title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the structural function of the chair and seat-support rails.
student: State the primary function of the chair and the structural role of the transverse seat-support rails.
instructor: The chair supports a seated person and transfers vertical load to the floor. The transverse rails support the seat and carry its load into the side frames.

title: Load Classification
learningObjectives: Classify the three specified load cases.
student: Classify the chair self-weight, ordinarily seated occupant, and person landing heavily on the seat as dead, live, or accidental loading.
instructor: The chair self-weight is dead load, the ordinarily seated occupant is live load, and landing heavily on the seat is the accidental load case.

title: Why the Falling Case Is Different
learningObjectives: Distinguish the given equivalent-static accidental load from an impact derivation.
student: Explain why a person landing heavily on the chair can produce greater demand than ordinary sitting. State how that event is represented in this problem.
instructor: A landing event can produce a larger, short-duration force than body weight alone. Here it is represented by the given 6.0 kN equivalent-static design load; students do not derive an impact force.

title: External Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace vertical chair load to the floor.
student: Trace the vertical load path from the occupant through the seat, rails, side frames, legs, and floor.
instructor: Occupant load enters the seat, is shared by the two transverse rails, transfers through the idealized rigid rail-to-frame joints into the side frames and legs, and is finally reacted by the floor.

title: Critical Component
learningObjectives: Identify the selected rail as the analysis component.
student: Identify the component selected for detailed analysis and explain why bending is relevant.
instructor: One transverse seat-support rail is selected. Its share of the centered vertical seat load produces shear and bending between the side frames.

title: Restraint Interpretation
learningObjectives: Interpret the instructor-assigned fixed-fixed idealization.
student: Describe the assigned end restraint for the selected rail and what it implies about end rotation and moment transfer.
instructor: Both rail ends are idealized as fixed, so translation and rotation are restrained and end moments can be transferred. This is an instructor-assigned idealization, not a verified description of photographed joints.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Select bending and flexural stress as the target response.
student: Identify the principal internal loading and stress response evaluated for the rail. Name important responses excluded from this model.
instructor: The assigned check evaluates beam bending and extreme-fiber flexural normal stress. It excludes weld stress, local buckling, fatigue, local contact, tipping, sliding, vibration, and impact dynamics.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Construct the one-rail fixed-fixed beam model.
student: Draw one rail as a fixed-fixed beam. Show its span, centered rail load, reactions, end moments, and square hollow cross-section.
instructor: A complete model shows span L, centered P_rail = P_A/2, equal vertical reactions, fixed-end moments of opposing sense, and the square hollow section defined by B and t.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State the assumptions that bound the teaching model.
student: State the assumptions used to reduce the real chair to the assigned one-rail beam model.
instructor: Assume a given equivalent-static accidental load, equal sharing by two equivalent rails, one straight prismatic fixed-fixed rail, centered point loading, rigid joints, a square hollow section, linear-elastic flexure through first yield, and small deformation. Exclude detailed impact, welds, local buckling, fatigue, contact, tipping, sliding, and vibration.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Sequence the rail-strength analysis.
student: Outline the calculation sequence from the load cases through rail loading, bending moment, section property, stress, factor of safety, allowable accidental load, and assessment.
instructor: Calculate the live load and compare load cases; divide the accidental load between rails; determine fixed-fixed reactions and M_max; calculate inside dimension, I, and c; calculate stress and factor of safety; then back-calculate allowable total load and assess the design.

title: Load Classification and Magnitudes
learningObjectives: Calculate and compare the three specified load magnitudes.
student: List the dead, live, and accidental load magnitudes. Calculate the seated-person live load and compare the accidental design load with it.
instructor: W_D is the specified dead load. W_L = mg = {{chair_live_load_N}} N. P_A is the given accidental load, which is {{chair_accidental_ratio}} times the calculated live load.

title: Given Accidental Design Load
learningObjectives: Use the accidental load as a given input without deriving impact.
student: State how the 6.0 kN accidental load is used and why no impact-force calculation is performed.
instructor: The 6.0 kN value is an instructor-specified equivalent-static total seat load used directly in the bending model. No fall height, stopping distance, contact duration, or dynamic amplification is supplied or derived.

title: Rail Load Sharing
learningObjectives: Determine one rail's load and reactions.
student: Using equal load sharing between two rails, calculate the centered load on one rail and its two vertical reactions.
instructor: P_rail = P_A/2 = {{chair_rail_load_N}} N ({{chair_rail_load_kN}} kN). Symmetry gives R_A = R_B = P_rail/2 = {{chair_reaction_N}} N ({{chair_reaction_kN}} kN).

title: Critical Bending Moment
learningObjectives: Calculate the maximum bending-moment magnitude.
student: For the centered point load on the fixed-fixed rail, determine the maximum bending-moment magnitude and identify where it occurs.
instructor: The support and midspan moment magnitudes are equal for this loading: |M|max = P_rail L/8 = {{chair_Mmax_Nmm}} N*mm = {{chair_Mmax_Nm}} N*m. The support moments are hogging and the midspan moment is sagging.

title: Square Hollow-Section Property
learningObjectives: Calculate the inside dimension, I, and c.
student: Calculate the inside dimension, centroidal second moment of area, and extreme-fiber distance for the square hollow rail.
instructor: b = B - 2t = {{chair_inside_dimension_mm}} mm; I = (B4-b4)/12 = {{chair_I_mm4}} mm4; c = B/2 = {{chair_c_mm}} mm.

title: Maximum Bending Stress
learningObjectives: Calculate the maximum flexural normal stress.
student: Calculate the maximum bending-stress magnitude in the rail using the flexure formula.
instructor: sigma_max = M_max c/I = {{chair_sigma_max_MPa}} MPa.

title: Strength Factor of Safety
learningObjectives: Compare calculated and required factors of safety.
student: Calculate the strength factor of safety against first yield and compare it with the required value.
instructor: n = S_y/sigma_max = {{chair_fos}}. The allowable stress based on the requirement is S_y/n_req = {{chair_allowable_stress_MPa}} MPa. {{chair_strength_assessment}}

title: Maximum Allowable Accidental Load
learningObjectives: Back-calculate the maximum total accidental load.
student: Using the required factor of safety, determine the maximum allowable total accidental seat load for this idealized two-rail system.
instructor: M_allow = (S_y/n_req)I/c = {{chair_Mallow_Nmm}} N*mm. Reversing M = (P_A/2)L/8 gives P_A,allow = {{chair_total_allowable_load_N}} N = {{chair_total_allowable_load_kN}} kN. {{chair_capacity_assessment}}

title: Capacity Comparison and Design Improvement
learningObjectives: Compare demand with capacity and propose a mechanics-based improvement.
student: Compare the given accidental load with the calculated allowable load. Recommend one direct mechanics-based change that would improve the rail strength margin.
instructor: {{chair_capacity_assessment}} Increasing B or t increases I and section modulus; reducing span or rail load reduces bending moment. Joint rigidity and load sharing must also be verified before treating the beam-model result as assembly capacity.

title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: State the result and limitations without overstating the model.
student: Prepare a concise engineering assessment stating the governing load case, rail stress, factor of safety, pass/fail result, allowable total accidental load, one recommended change, and the model limitations.
instructor: {{chair_engineering_assessment}}
